h1: 10 Wild Chinese EV Sports Cars That Deserve Your Attention

contentBlocks.text: Most people expect a list of electric vehicles to be full of SUVs and commuter cars with massive screens and quiet motors. It is easy to think that EVs are only meant for basic daily driving. However, the car market in China has changed significantly.

While drivers in the U.S. are still waiting for the Tesla Roadster to be released, Chinese automakers have started building much more than just basic commuter cars. They are now making high-performance vehicles, including carbon-fiber track cars and hypercars that use four motors. They are also producing small, lightweight roadsters that focus on how the car handles.
Because of trade policies and tariffs, these cars cannot be bought in the U.S. right now. Even if they are not available here, they are still worth looking at for anyone who follows the car industry.
Here are 10 of the most interesting electric sports cars coming out of China today.
1. Hongqi S9 (0-60 mph: 1.9s)
2. GAC Hyptec SSR (0-60 mph: 1.9s)
3. Xiaomi SU7 Ultra (0-60 mph: 1.98s)
5. Denza Z (0-60 mph: <2.0s)
4. Yangwang U9 (0-60 mph: 2.3s)
6. Arcfox GT (0-60 mph: 2.6s)
7. NIO EP9 (0-60 mph: 2.7s)
9. Aion Hyper GT (0-60 mph: 3.7s)
10. Neta GT (0-60 mph: 3.7s)
1Hongqi S9
1,400 HP | 1.9 seconds
Let’s start at the absolute top of the food chain with a car that sounds like a glitch in the Matrix.

Hongqi is the oldest, most traditional automotive brand in China. For decades, their sole purpose was building massive, armored, ultra-luxury limousines to ferry around top government officials and visiting heads of state. They are essentially the Rolls-Royce of China—deeply conservative, steeped in history, and completely focused on the back seat.

So, what happens when a brand like that decides to build a hypercar? You get the S9, a plug-in hybrid rocket ship that looks like it flew straight out of a European design studio. In fact, it basically did. Hongqi hired Walter de Silva—the legendary former head of VW Group design who penned icons like the Audi R8 and Lamborghini Egoista—to shape this thing.

Underneath the gorgeous carbon-fiber bodywork sits a twin-turbo V8 paired with three electric motors. The math? A mind-numbing 1,400 horsepower, a top speed of 250 mph, and a 0-60 mph sprint of 1.9 seconds. To put that in perspective, that’s Bugatti Chiron performance coming from a brand better known for parade cars.

Now, full disclosure from the editor's desk: the S9 has been a bit of a ghost. It went through a messy saga trying to set up production in Italy's "Motor Valley" near Ferrari before production shifted back home to China, making customer deliveries incredibly rare and shrouded in mystery. But whether you can easily spot one on the street or not, the S9 did its job. It was the opening shot that proved China wasn't just here to build sensible commuter cars—they were coming for the hypercar crown.
2GAC Hyptec SSR
1,225 HP | 1.9 seconds

The GAC Hyptec SSR is quite different from other high-end cars that never seem to actually make it to the road. It was previously called the Hyper SSR, and it is a real production car being built on an assembly line right now. You can actually buy one today, though not in the US. It is not just a concept car or a limited edition for the super wealthy. It is China’s first mass-produced electric supercar.

GAC is a huge company that mostly builds standard SUVs for families. When they launched their premium brand, Hyptec, they wanted to make a big impact. They decided to do that by building a car with 1,225 horsepower to challenge the traditional European supercar makers.

The SSR stands for Super, Sport, and Race. It looks like a classic exotic car, with a wedge shape and automatic scissor doors. The car has a full carbon-fiber body and uses a three-motor, all-wheel-drive system that puts down a lot of power. The top-tier version can go from 0 to 60 mph in 1.9 seconds, which makes it extremely fast.
To manage all that power, GAC worked on custom tires and carbon-ceramic brakes. They even adapted some technology from the aviation industry to help the car handle the speed.

The most interesting part is the price. It starts at around 186,000 dollars in China. While that is expensive for a typical car, it is very low for a supercar. It provides performance similar to the Rimac Nevera for about a tenth of the cost. It is a clear sign that China can produce a world-class sports car without needing a famous European brand name.
3Xiaomi SU7 Ultra
1,548 HP | 1.98 seconds

Apple spent ten years trying to build an electric car before they finally gave up on the project. At the same time, Xiaomi, a company known for phones and appliances, successfully made a sedan that is actually faster than a Bugatti. While the SU7 Ultra might look like a typical four-door car, it was built specifically for high performance.

Xiaomi proved what the car could do by taking a prototype to the Nürburgring track in Germany, where it finished a lap in 6:22.091. The production version later set a record for its category with a time of 7:04.957. The car has even caught the eye of Ford CEO Jim Farley, who mentioned he has been driving a regular SU7 in the U.S. and really likes it.

The specs are a big part of the story. The car has three electric motors that produce 1,548 horsepower and 1,305 lb-ft of torque. This lets it hit 60 mph in just 1.98 seconds, which is faster than a Tesla Model S Plaid. Because the car is heavy at 5,200 pounds, Xiaomi added carbon-fiber parts to improve aerodynamics and used Bilstein dampers and carbon-ceramic brakes to keep it under control.

In China, the SU7 Ultra is priced around $114,000. This is quite low compared to performance sedans from European companies. It shows that tech companies are now becoming serious players in the car industry.
4Denza Z
1,560 HP | <2.0 seconds

The Denza Z is BYD’s attempt to compete with high-end brands like Porsche and Maserati. While Denza started as a joint project with Mercedes-Benz, BYD now owns the brand entirely. This new model is a carbon-fiber sports car with four seats, available as either a hardtop or a convertible. Its performance specs are similar to what you would expect from a hypercar.

The car uses a three-motor system that produces a total of 1,560 horsepower. There is one 500 kW motor on the front axle and two 340 kW motors at the back. This power allows the car to reach 60 mph in under two seconds, and with the optional track package, it can hit 217 mph.

It was designed to handle well, not just go fast in a straight line. Since each motor can work independently, the car can use torque vectoring to improve cornering and perform maneuvers like tank turns. It also shares an active suspension system with the expensive Yangwang U9, which uses magnetic damping to keep the car flat through corners.

Wolfgang Egger, a designer who previously worked for Lamborghini and Alfa Romeo, oversaw the car's look. It features an aggressive style with frameless doors and a large wing on the back. Even though it has high-end materials and extreme power, it is expected to be much cheaper than European electric luxury cars. The Denza Z is a clear sign that 1,500 horsepower is becoming more common and accessible.
5Yangwang U9
1,287 HP | 2.3 seconds

If you still have doubts about what Chinese car companies can do, the Yangwang U9 might change your perspective. This is a 233,000 dollar electric hypercar from BYD’s luxury brand. It comes with four electric motors that deliver 1,287 horsepower, but it is actually more famous for its suspension than its speed. The car uses a system called DiSus-X that allows each wheel to move independently. This lets the car jump off the ground, move in sync with music, or even stay stable at high speeds on only three wheels if a tire blows out.

While some of these features feel like party tricks, the performance is real. The standard model can go from 0 to 60 mph in 2.3 seconds. To show it is more than just a heavy show car, Yangwang tested a high-performance version in Germany. It reached a top speed of 308 mph and finished a lap at the Nürburgring in less than seven minutes.

The biggest drawback is the weight. The car uses BYD’s lithium iron phosphate Blade battery, which is more affordable but much heavier than what other hypercars use. This brings the total weight to over 5,400 pounds. Because it is so heavy, it feels more like a powerful, fast machine than a light and nimble sports car. Even so, for the price, it provides technology and speed that usually cost millions of dollars when buying from traditional supercar manufacturers.
6Arcfox GT
1,005 HP | 2.6 seconds

Even though brands like BYD and Xiaomi get most of the attention today, BAIC’s high-end brand, Arcfox, was one of the first Chinese companies to build an electric hypercar. They first showed the Arcfox GT at the Geneva Motor Show to prove they could make a refined, high-performance car that could compete with European models.

The car uses a carbon-fiber frame and a lightweight aluminum structure for the battery, which keeps the total weight under 4,100 pounds. For an electric car with this much power, that is relatively light. The standard Street Edition has four electric motors that produce 1,005 horsepower, allowing it to go from 0 to 60 mph in about 2.6 seconds. They also made a Track Edition for even more power, using a six-motor setup to reach 1,609 horsepower.

To make sure it handles well on a track and doesn't just go fast in a straight line, the car has a balanced 50:50 weight distribution and an active suspension system. It also uses large carbon-ceramic brakes that can bring the car to a full stop from 60 mph in 115 feet.

The main downside is that the Arcfox GT is very expensive and hard to find. It was originally priced at around $1.1 million and was never intended for regular production. Instead, it was a limited project meant to show off the company's engineering capabilities. While you probably won't see one driving around, it was an important step in showing that Chinese car manufacturers could build high-performance electric vehicles long before it became a popular trend.
7NIO EP9
1,341 HP | 2.6 seconds

Before NIO was known for its battery-swapping stations and luxury EVs, the company wanted to do something that would get everyone's attention. In 2016, they launched the EP9. This wasn't just another electric car with quick acceleration; it was built specifically for the track and designed to break world records.

To show what it was capable of, NIO took the EP9 to the Nürburgring in 2017. It finished a lap in 6 minutes and 45.90 seconds, making it the fastest street-legal production car at that track for a period of time. The car has four electric motors, one for each wheel, producing a total of 1,341 horsepower. It goes from 0 to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and can reach a top speed of 194 mph.

Aerodynamics is what really sets the EP9 apart. At 143 mph, it generates about 5,395 pounds of downforce, which is double what a Formula 1 car produces. This helps it handle turns with 3.3 Gs of lateral force, which is far more than most people could physically handle. It also uses a battery system that can be swapped out in the pit lane in a few minutes, which was basically the early version of the technology NIO uses in its regular cars now.

You probably won't ever see an EP9 on the road, though. NIO only made a few of them, costing about $1.48 million each, and they were mostly sold to the company's first investors and wealthy tech figures. It was never intended for the general public. Instead, it was meant to prove that NIO could handle serious engineering right from the start.
8SC01
429 HP | 2.9 seconds

Most electric cars coming out of China these days are loaded with huge touchscreens and self-driving tech. The SC01 takes the opposite approach. Built by a small firm called Small Sports Car with backing from Xiaomi, this two-door coupe gets rid of the usual tech bloat. The designers focused on just one thing: making a lightweight, affordable car that handles well.

The look is inspired by classic Italian rally cars like the Lancia Stratos. To keep the weight low, the company used a simple tubular frame and skipped the large screens and driver-assist systems that usually add bulk. It weighs just over 3,000 pounds, which is lighter than a Porsche 718 Cayman and very light for an electric vehicle with two motors.

It is still quite powerful despite the low weight. The car uses an all-wheel-drive system with two motors producing 429 horsepower. Because the battery is mounted right behind the seats, it feels like a traditional mid-engine sports car with a low driving position. It can go from 0 to 60 mph in about 2.9 seconds.

The price is one of its most appealing features. In China, it starts at around $31,500, which is less than a Mazda Miata. It has also started appearing in Europe in small numbers. The SC01 is proof that an electric sports car does not have to be heavy or expensive to be fun to drive.
9Aion Hyper GT
340 HP | 3.7 seconds

If you want a car with scissor doors but still need to go grocery shopping or fit adults in the back seats, the Aion Hyper GT is a solid option. It is built by GAC’s premium brand, which is the same group that made the SSR hypercar. The idea behind this sedan was to combine the look of a supercar with a design that actually works for everyday life.

The car is very aerodynamic, with a drag coefficient of only 0.197. It has a front grille that opens automatically to cool the brakes when you are driving fast, and a rear wing that pops out to help with stability. The most obvious feature, though, is the front doors that swing upward, which gives the car a much more exotic look than a typical sedan.

The top-spec version is rear-wheel drive and produces 340 horsepower. Since the power goes to the back wheels, it handles more like a traditional sports sedan. It can reach 60 mph in about 3.7 seconds, which is quite fast. It also supports very quick charging, allowing you to add about 280 miles of range in 15 minutes.

Inside, the cabin is simple and focused on technology. It uses high-quality materials and includes a large infotainment screen along with a 23-speaker sound system. In China, the price ranges from $30,000 to $47,000 depending on the version. It ends up being a practical choice for someone who wants supercar styling and modern features without the high price tag of a European electric luxury car.
10Neta GT
462 HP | 3.7 seconds

For a long time, two-door sports coupes like the Ford Mustang or BMW 4 Series were popular because they looked sporty but were still practical enough to drive every day. Now, Neta has taken that same idea and turned it into an electric car designed for people on a budget.

The Neta GT does not look like a futuristic spaceship. It sticks to a traditional design with a long hood and a sloping roofline. It is a 2+2 coupe, which means it has small back seats for extra passengers or bags. With both a trunk and a frunk, it is easy to live with as a daily driver.

The base model is a simple rear-wheel-drive car, but the all-wheel-drive performance version is much faster. It has 462 horsepower and can go from 0 to 60 mph in about 3.7 seconds. To help with handling, it comes with a sport-tuned suspension and Michelin tires to keep it stable through corners.

The interior features a large 17.6-inch touchscreen and a panoramic sunroof that makes the cabin feel more open. The most interesting part of the Neta GT is the price. In China, the high-performance model starts at around $32,000, while the base version is closer to $25,000. It is a good example of how the affordable sports coupe is changing rather than disappearing.
The Bottom Line

Looking at this list, it is clear that the old hierarchy of the car world is falling apart. For over a hundred years, if you wanted a car with top-tier speed and engineering, you had to go to a few famous European brands. That is not the case anymore. What is interesting is how Chinese companies are taking several different paths to get into the performance market.

Some companies, like Xiaomi, are showing that a background in tech and software can lead to fast cars much quicker than traditional automakers can react. At the same time, big manufacturers like BYD and GAC are using their massive production scale to build cars with over a thousand horsepower for much less money than people used to pay. Then there are brands like Neta, which are making affordable electric sports cars that Western companies have basically given up on.

From powerful sedans breaking track records to small, affordable roadsters, these cars show that electric vehicles are not just for basic commuting. Chinese companies are now at the center of the conversation about performance cars.
